messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Publisher
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Vulnerability: Being naked, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Vignette:
Amir is a thirty-four-year-old married man who works as a publisher in a mid-sized city. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he agreed that something had to change. He had been a steady, even-keeled person before, but for the past eighteen months he had become someone he barely recognised. The trouble began on an ordinary Tuesday evening when his wife, Leila, was driving home from a late shift at the hospital where she worked as a nurse. A driver ran a red light and struck her car broadside. Amir received the call from the emergency room while he was still at the office. By the time he arrived, she was in surgery, and he spent the next four hours in a windowless waiting room, hearing only fragments of information from a nurse who seemed to be speaking a language he could not quite understand. He remembers the sound of a television mounted high on the wall, playing a news program he could not follow, and the way the fluorescent lights hummed. He remembers the smell of antiseptic and the feel of the plastic chair armrest under his palm. But these pieces do not connect into a coherent story. When he tries to recall that evening, he gets only disconnected fragments: the hum, the smell, the nurse’s mouth moving, the phone in his hand. They arrive like a film that plays over and over, but always out of order, and he cannot make them stop.

Leila survived, but her recovery was slow and complicated. She is home now, mostly healed, though she still has a limp and tires easily. Amir is grateful beyond words, but the relief did not bring peace. Instead, his life has become a landscape of hidden dangers. He studies people’s faces and body language constantly, scanning for threat in every interaction. On the bus, which he used to take without a second thought, he now finds himself cataloguing the passengers—who looks agitated, who is holding something that could become a weapon, who is standing too close. He notices potential weapons everywhere: a heavy keychain, a glass bottle, a man’s belt. He has come to believe that danger is always one misread face away, and that his vigilance is the only thing keeping him and Leila safe. He avoids unfamiliar places entirely, because he cannot assess the threat level in a space he does not already know. This has narrowed his world considerably. He no longer agrees to work dinners or industry events, and his publisher colleagues have started to notice his absences. He tells them he is busy, but the truth is that he cannot walk into a restaurant he has never visited without his heart hammering and his eyes darting to every exit.

The most confusing and shameful trigger for Amir is being naked. He cannot explain it, but when he undresses for a shower or changes clothes, a wave of vulnerability washes over him that makes him feel as exposed as he did in that hospital waiting room. He has started showering with the bathroom door locked and the lights off, because the feeling is too intense otherwise. He is also acutely aware that when he is very tired or exhausted, his guard drops, and the fragmented memories come more frequently and with greater force. He hears things—the hum of the fluorescent light, the nurse’s voice, the television—as though they are happening in the room with him. On those nights, he cannot sleep, and the next day he is even more exhausted, and the cycle tightens.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a moment of rupture. Last week, Leila asked him to pick up a prescription from a pharmacy in a neighbourhood they had never visited. He refused. She asked why, and he could not tell her the truth—that he could not possibly assess the danger in that place, that he would spend the entire trip watching for threats, that he would come home shaking and useless. She looked at him with a sadness he had seen before, and he realised that his avoidance had become a wall between them. He is afraid of what will happen if he lets his guard down, but he is also afraid of losing the life they fought so hard to rebuild. He hopes that therapy will teach him how to stop scanning every face, how to walk into a room without cataloguing the exits, and how to feel safe in his own skin again.
